name: Karl Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Fenwick Growers. We grow leeks, broccoli and savoy cabbage for one of the big supermarkets, about four hundred hectares. Right now it's leek season, so I'm out at half six with the harvest crew, then in the packhouse in the afternoon, trimming and bagging. Three leeks to a bag, each one the same length, or the supermarket sends the whole pallet back.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's the same every day. You know where you stand. What wears me out is the cold, your hands in wet leeks at seven in the morning in November. And the speed. Everyone on the line is faster than me. Marek, who's been there nine years, does three bags to my two.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI or computer tools in the work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No. Not at work, not at home. My brother keeps telling me to ask his phone things and I just don't. The packhouse has a camera that checks the bags for size, but I don't touch that, the supervisor does. I just bag.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nothing, really. It doesn't come up. If someone asked, I'd say fine, a better search engine, I'll stick to the old one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, nothing changes for me and that's what I want. I've got the job, I've got the flat with my brother, I know my route in. I'd like more money, sure, but I've got about two weeks saved and I'm not going to go chasing something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Do the leeks till March, broccoli from June. Maybe ask for the forklift ticket, because forklift drivers in the packhouse get a bit more an hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the one I'd pick if I could pick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What stops you asking for the forklift ticket now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing, really, if I'm honest. I just haven't. There's a test, and I don't like tests. I'll probably ask in spring. I said that last spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who decides how things go at Fenwick, as you see it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The supermarket. They decide the price, the size of the leek, when they want it, how it's packed. Fenwick just does what they're told. So does everyone. I'm not saying it's right or wrong, it's just how it works.

S0.say: I'd say nothing much, because it doesn't come up. If asked, I'd say it's a better search engine and I'll stick with the old one.
S0.think: Nothing changes for me and that's what I want. I've got the job, the flat with my brother and about two weeks saved, and I'm not going chasing something new.
S0.do: Carries on with leeks until March and broccoli from June. Thinks about asking for the forklift licence in spring, for slightly better pay, as he did last year.
S0.feel: Calm. This is the future he would choose.
S0.quote: I'll probably ask in spring. I said that last spring.
S0.fieldNote: Very short, plain answers, and a clear preference for routine. He laughed at himself over the forklift licence. He sees the supermarket as the real boss but doesn't treat that as a grievance, just a fact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's hard for young people, but it's always been hard. I got this job because my cousin knew the supervisor. That's how it works round here. Fewer beginners just means more of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'm not sure what it means. I'm still the beginner, kind of, three years in and still slow. If a task goes, it'll probably be the packing, because that's the bit that's already half machines. And that's my afternoons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Try to get faster on the line, so I'm not the obvious one. Maybe finally do the forklift ticket. I wouldn't look at other jobs, there aren't any, not round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not much, but a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would losing the afternoons in the packhouse mean in money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half my hours in winter. The field work alone doesn't make a full week from November to February. I'd be on about half pay. Rent's half of what I earn now, so that doesn't work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If that happened, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ask Fenwick for something else, cleaning, the yard, anything. Then my brother would cover my half of the rent for a bit, I suppose. He wouldn't like it. He'd say I told you, learn the phone stuff.

S1.say: I'd say it's hard for young people, but it always has been. I got my job because my cousin knew the supervisor, and fewer beginners just means more of that.
S1.think: I'm not sure what it means, but if a task goes it'll probably be packing, because that's already half machines. That's my afternoons, and half my winter hours.
S1.do: Tries to get faster on the packing line so he's not the obvious one to cut, and finally does the forklift licence. Doesn't look at other jobs, because there are none nearby.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy, in the background.
S1.quote: If a task goes, it'll probably be the packing, because that's the bit that's already half machines. And that's my afternoons.
S1.fieldNote: He thinks in hours rather than jobs: losing a task means losing half his winter hours. He didn't blame anyone and treated connections as the normal way into work. His brother keeps pushing him toward technology and he keeps resisting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's bad for them, but it's not us. Nobody in the packhouse does office work. I'd keep out of the politics. They all shout and then nothing changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's mostly fine for me. Fenwick's office is three people, they might lose one. The supermarket's office might use AI to do the orders, which could mean the orders change faster, more last-minute stuff. That would be annoying, not the end of the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. Keep working. Maybe put a bit more aside, twenty a week if I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. For other people more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said orders might change faster. What would that look like on a normal day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We already get calls at two in the afternoon saying they want another two thousand bags by five. If a computer's doing the orders, maybe that's every day. That means staying late, which means overtime, which actually I wouldn't mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you know who works in an office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother. He does customer service for an energy company, from home. He uses all the AI stuff. Funny if he's the one who goes and I'm the one who didn't learn any of it.

S2.say: I'd say it's bad for office workers, but it isn't us, because nobody in the packhouse does office work. I'd keep out of the politics, since they shout and nothing changes.
S2.think: It's mostly fine for me. The supermarket might use AI for orders and change them at the last minute more often, which would be annoying but not the end of the world.
S2.do: Keeps working as normal and puts aside about twenty a week if he can. Takes any extra overtime that last-minute orders bring.
S2.feel: A little uneasy, mostly on behalf of other people.
S2.quote: Funny if he's the one who goes and I'm the one who didn't learn any of it.
S2.fieldNote: He noticed a real knock-on effect: AI ordering at the supermarket could mean more last-minute rush orders, which he sees as overtime rather than a threat. The irony that his tech-savvy brother is more exposed than he is clearly amused him. He stays away from politics on purpose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a mess, and somebody should sort it out, but I don't know who. The government, I suppose. Not my area.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the bit that worries me is people having less money. If loads of people lose jobs, they buy cheaper veg. The supermarket squeezes Fenwick, Fenwick squeezes us. Our rent's going up too, the landlord's already hinted, and with house prices booming he'll want more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep my head down. Do as many hours as they give me. Cut what I can, which isn't much, I don't go out a lot. If the rent goes up, I'd talk to my brother about moving somewhere smaller, out of town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not about the job, about the money around the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'somebody should sort it out'. If you had to choose, what should they do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Make sure the people who lose jobs get something, I suppose, but not so much that nobody works. Something in the middle. I'd want to see it working somewhere else first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym. I pay for a gym in town I go to twice a month. My brother keeps saying cancel it. In this one, I'd finally cancel it.

S3.say: I'd say it's a mess and somebody should sort it out, probably the government. It's not something I'd get into myself.
S3.think: What worries me is people having less money and buying cheaper vegetables, so the supermarket squeezes Fenwick and Fenwick squeezes us. Our rent is going up too, with house prices booming.
S3.do: Keeps his head down and takes all the hours offered. Cancels his gym membership and talks to his brother about moving somewhere smaller out of town if the rent rises.
S3.feel: Anxious about the money around the job rather than the job itself.
S3.quote: The supermarket squeezes Fenwick, Fenwick squeezes us.
S3.fieldNote: A pragmatic, middle-ground answer on policy: support for people who lose jobs, but only once it's proven elsewhere. He traced the pressure from shoppers down the supply chain to himself in one sentence. The gym membership he barely uses was a nice small detail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks for staying with me. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not going to work in a leek field. Mud, cold, leeks all different sizes. I'd say that loud, to anyone. That's what we'd all say in the packhouse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: But between us, I've already seen one. Last summer a company brought a weeding robot to the broccoli, a thing on wheels with cameras that hoes between the plants. It was slow, but it didn't stop for lunch. The supermarket already tells us how long a leek has to be. Next it'll tell us who picks it, and it won't be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Honestly, I'd wait and see, because I don't know what else to do. I'd ask the supervisor if there'd be jobs looking after the machines. I'd probably say no if he said yes, because I don't know computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad. Scared, if I'm honest. I don't like saying that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd probably turn down a job looking after the machines. Can you say more about why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd be bad at it and then I'd get let go from that instead. At least now I know I can bag leeks. I'd rather be slow at a thing I know than useless at a thing I don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you go if Fenwick didn't need you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's nothing near. The meat plant, maybe, if they're not robots too. Or move to the city with my brother's help, which I've never wanted. I've lived here all my life.

S4.say: I'd say robots won't work in a leek field, with the mud, the cold and leeks all different sizes. That's what everyone in the packhouse would say.
S4.think: Privately I've already seen a weeding robot with cameras working our broccoli, slow but never stopping for lunch. The supermarket sets the leek length already, and next it'll decide who picks it.
S4.do: Waits to see what happens and asks his supervisor whether there will be jobs looking after the machines, though he would probably turn one down. Considers the meat plant or moving to the city with his brother's help.
S4.quote: The supermarket already tells us how long a leek has to be. Next it'll tell us who picks it, and it won't be me.
S4.fieldNote: The biggest say and think gap in his interview: publicly 'it won't work', privately he has already watched a robot weeder. His resistance to technology runs deep enough that he'd likely refuse a machine-minding job. He named fear directly and then seemed embarrassed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The last one, the robots. It's the only one where there's nothing left for me to do. What would help, I don't know. Time, I suppose. A few years' warning, and someone actually showing me the machine slowly, not a manual. I'd try then.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the foreign workers. Half our harvest crew come for the season from abroad. If robots come, they lose it first, and nobody here even knows their names. I know Marek's. That's about it.

headlineQuote: The supermarket already tells us how long a leek has to be. Next it'll tell us who picks it, and it won't be me.
portrait: Karl Ibrahim is a 27-year-old field and packhouse worker on a vegetable farm that grows leeks, broccoli and cabbage for a supermarket. He shares a rented flat with his brother, has about two weeks of savings, and has never used AI tools and doesn't want to. He sees the supermarket as the real boss and treats that as a plain fact rather than a grievance. Through the office scenarios he worries mostly about rent and cheaper shopping squeezing his pay. In the robot scenario his public confidence covers real fear, because he has already watched a weeding robot work, and he admits he might turn down a job minding the machines.
biggestWorry: The fast robots scenario, because it's the only one where there would be nothing left for him to do.
whatWouldHelp: A few years' warning and someone showing him the new machines slowly and in person, not through a manual.
